html:
Poland is a country on the North European Plain, between Germany and Russia. Its borders have moved more than almost any other in Europe, and the map shows several versions: the Piast kingdom from 1000 to 1300, the shrunken state of 1783, the republic between the world wars, and the country shifted west after 1945.

Prince Mieszko I of the Piast dynasty brought Poland into Christian Europe with the baptism of 966, and his son was crowned king in 1025. After 1138 the land split among princes, and in 1241 the Mongol invasion struck it. Casimir III, the Great, rebuilt a strong kingdom in the 1300s.

In 1385 Poland joined with Lithuania, and the two became the joint state of Poland-Lithuania, formally the Commonwealth from 1569. Its nobles elected their kings and could block laws. Weak and surrounded, it lost a first slice of land in 1772, which is the state shown on the 1783 map. It passed the Constitution of 3 May 1791, but Russia, Prussia and Austria finished the partitions in 1795.

Poland came back in 1918. In 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union invaded it, and the Second World War killed about a sixth of its people, including most of its three million Jews. In 1945 its borders were moved west. The Solidarity trade union led the challenge to communist rule, which ended in 1989. Poland joined the European Union in 2004.
